svg.title: Plans for a rainy day
svg.desc: Original family-manga illustration: umbrella, related to Plans for a rainy day.

text.tspan: A good way to change our plans combines practical structure with an awareness of other people. Neither a rigid plan nor
complete improvisation is sufficient on its own; both need to be judged in context.
The practical case is straightforward: a backup plan makes a change less disappointing. Consider how we choose a museum when rain makes the outdoor
walk uncomfortable. The benefit is not merely efficiency. A modest arrangement prevents avoidable confusion, leaving attention available for the activity itself
rather than for problems that could have been anticipated.
Consideration adds a second, equally important dimension: telling other people early helps everyone adjust. In this situation, we send a clear message about
the new meeting place before anyone leaves home. A decision can be convenient for one person while creating difficulty for another, so its value depends
partly on whose needs it recognises.
The most useful approach therefore brings structure and consideration together. Preparation establishes a workable starting point; attention to other people
keeps it responsive. Success should be assessed by how well the arrangement serves the experience, rather than by how closely events follow the original
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a focused main idea. Develop one supporting reason in each body paragraph, with a concrete example. Conclude by connecting the two
reasons without introducing a new argument. Use the structure as a model; write about an experience of your own.
What two reasons support the main idea? Explain one example. (Model: The two reasons are that a backup plan makes a change less disappointing and that telling other
people early helps everyone adjust. One example is that we choose a museum when rain makes the outdoor walk uncomfortable.)
